resources.title: Conservation Resources
resources.subtitle: Understand your legal responsibilities, learn how to prevent collisions, and know exactly what to do if you encounter a wildlife emergency on the road.
resources.actDesc: India's primary law for the protection of plants and animal species. Under this act, hunting, harming, or accidentally killing scheduled animals (like Tigers, Leopards, Elephants) is a severe criminal offense.
resources.penalty1: Hitting a Schedule I animal (e.g., Tiger, Elephant) can lead to 3 to 7 years in prison and a minimum fine of ₹10,000.
resources.penalty2: Fleeing the scene without reporting the incident is considered poaching/hunting under the law.
resources.penalty3: Confiscation of the vehicle involved in the collision is standard procedure.
resources.actionSubtitle: If you witness or are involved in a wildlife collision, follow these steps immediately:
resources.step1Desc: Never approach or touch an injured wild animal. They may lash out in panic, or carry zoonotic diseases.
resources.step2Desc: Turn on your hazard lights. If safe, place warning triangles to alert other drivers and prevent secondary accidents.
resources.step3Desc: Call the local Forest Department or emergency services immediately with your exact GPS location.
resources.step4Desc: Once safe, log the incident on WILDMAP to help conservationists track the hotspot.
resources.preventionTip1: Drive under 40 km/h when passing through recognized forest corridors or national park peripheries.
resources.preventionTip2: Avoid night driving in wildlife zones. Many fatal collisions involve nocturnal animals.
resources.preventionTip3: Do not litter. Food thrown from cars attracts animals to the highway edge.
resources.footerDesc: Every animal lost on the road is a blow to India's fragile biodiversity. By slowing down, staying alert, and reporting incidents, you become the first line of defense in wildlife conservation.
